adversarial_test_results.prompt: For most of the nineteenth century a lighthouse keeper's day began before dawn. The keeper climbed the spiral stair with a can of oil, trimmed the wick, polished the lens, and logged the weather in a ledger that would later be read by inspectors who arrived by boat once a season. Fog was the worst of it. A lamp could throw its beam thirty miles on a clear night, but fog swallowed light within a few hundred yards, and so the keepers also kept a bell, a horn, or a small cannon that they fired at intervals through the night. Neighbours on shore complained about the noise; the keepers complained about the neighbours. Both complaints appear, in almost identical wording, in the correspondence of the Northern Lights Board between 1861 and 1889. The buildings themselves were engineered for wind. Walls were doubled, mortared with lime, and tapered toward the top so that gusts would slide past instead of pressing. Windows were small and set deep. The lantern room at the summit was a cage of iron and glass, and in a gale the whole structure would hum at a pitch that keepers described in their journals as a low whistle or, in one memorable entry, as the sound of a distant choir that would not stop. Supplying such places was its own trade. Tenders arrived with flour, salt beef, lamp oil, and mail, and left with the keeper's reports. In winter the sea could close for weeks. Keepers planted small gardens in sheltered hollows, kept goats for milk, and traded with passing fishermen. Some stayed for decades; others lasted a single season and resigned by the next boat. By the early twentieth century the economics had changed. Acetylene and then electric lamps reduced the labour of tending a flame, and automated clockwork replaced the keeper who wound the mechanism every few hours. The great conversion came after the Second World War, when remote monitoring made it possible to run a light from an office on the mainland. Keepers were pensioned off, and the cottages passed to preservation trusts, seabird biologists, and, briefly and controversially, to holiday lets. What remains is a peculiar kind of archive. Ledgers, brass fittings, and hand-drawn charts sit in county record offices alongside oral histories recorded in the 1970s, when the last generation of keepers was still alive and willing to talk. Historians have used these sources to argue about labour, about the technology of visibility, and about the strange solitude of a job whose entire purpose was to be seen and never to be visited. The arguments are unresolved, as arguments about small institutions usually are, but the record itself is remarkably complete, and anyone willing to read a hundred years of weather notes will find in them a slow, patient account of a coast changing shape.
